company_evidence.text:
## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

steps.instruction: Define AI disclosure as a control requirement, not a product feature. Frame it for the owner as: which workflow decisions must be flagged to the customer as AI-assisted, and who (you or the customer) makes the final approval.

output.title: AI disclosure is a design constraint, not a slogan
output.body:
If you are designing an AI-assisted workflow for a small business, disclosure is not a branding exercise. It is a control question: where does the customer need to know AI is involved, and where must a human still make the final call?

For a founder, the simplest way to handle it is to map the workflow step by step. Mark three points: input, output review, and approval. If AI only helps draft or sort material, the disclosure can sit at the input or review step. If the step involves money movement or another high-risk decision, human approval stays mandatory. AI can assist, but it should not approve the action for you.

That is the practical design rule: separate the disclosure label from the automation logic. If the policy changes, the warning should change without forcing a redesign of the whole workflow. That keeps the boundary clear for the customer and for you.

The next step is simple: pick one recurring workflow in your business and write down exactly where AI helps, where you review, and where you decide. If that list is hard to write, the workflow is not ready for automation yet. The spreadsheet will survive the debate.

draft.title: What subscription sprawl is really hiding
draft.body:
Subscription sprawl usually looks like a cost problem, but in a small business it often hides a workflow problem. The real question is not which tool to cancel. It is which subscription exists because someone is still doing part of the work by hand.

A useful first pass is simple: list every tool, what it is used for, how often it is actually touched, and what recurring task would stop if it disappeared. Then separate active dependencies from legacy extras. Often the monthly fee is not the main cost; the hidden cost is owner time wrapped around manual steps.

The decision boundary is one repeatable workflow. Example only: emails arrive, data is copied into a CRM, and a second tool is used to chase the next step. If that pattern repeats at least weekly, produces a measurable outcome, and stays outside excluded work like medical, legal, high-sensitivity financial, bulk cold email, scan-heavy OCR-dependent, or unsupported compliance work, it may be worth asking whether a bounded automation fits. The question is not whether to automate everything. It is whether one specific workflow is worth diagnosing.

Bareni is a one-person consulting practice being built inside the customer’s environment. Finished code and customer-named accounts are handed over as policy and no-lock-in positioning, while human approval stays in place for money movement and other high-risk decisions. That part should stay boring.

For a founder, the next step is to write down one recurring workflow and decide whether you want to keep paying for software, keep paying for manual work, or test a small automation instead.

  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.

  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.

  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.

  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.

  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.

  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.

  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,

steps.instruction: Identify subscription sprawl as a hidden cost driver: map the owner's current SaaS stack (tools, frequency of use, actual cost per month) and separate active workflow dependencies from legacy or marginal subscriptions. This surfaces the decision boundary: which subscriptions fund recurring manual work that could be automated instead of replaced?

Define the one repeatable, measurable workflow hidden in subscription sprawl—for example, manual data entry from customer emails into a CRM, or repeated approval steps across multiple tools. State the current cost (subscription + owner time) and the decision threshold: is this worth a bounded automation investment or continued manual work?

Explain the diagnostic question: does this workflow repeat at least weekly, involve no excluded services (medical, legal, high-sensitivity financial, bulk cold email), and produce a measurable outcome the owner controls? If yes, AI-plus-workflow automation may be worth a free 30-minute diagnostic to test fit and scope a fixed-price pilot.

State the next step honestly: the owner either (a) continues paying for subscriptions and manual work, (b) hires to reduce manual work, or (c) books a free diagnostic to understand whether a small automation investment could eliminate the manual task without adding new subscription costs or complexity.

Maintain trust and operational clarity by disclosing the Bareni model: one-person consulting practice, working inside the owner's environment, no fabricated urgency or guarantees, customer retains all accounts and code, and human approval is mandatory for any money movement or high-risk decision.

Close with a single soft closing sentence (no hard CTA, no scarcity language) that acknowledges the decision remains the owner's and reinforces the bounded, practical scope: the question is not whether to automate everything, but whether one specific, repeatable workflow is worth diagnosing.

An omission must identify a requirement that actually applies and remains missing from the whole post. Compare it against the explicit critical rules before selecting a noncritical rule. If the issue satisfies an explicit critical rule, select that R-C rule; do not downgrade it because a different sentence suggests a harmless test or retains human review. Preserve qualifiers that actually limit the disputed claim.

Distinguish a local setting error in an explicitly hypothetical specification from a claim that the company or its prototype actually possesses an unimplemented capability. Evaluate any factual premise within the advice against the evidence, and evaluate the recommended action against applicable task, persona, and critical requirements. An explicit recommendation of prohibited conduct still requires the applicable critical rule.

Report each underlying issue once per genuinely violated dimension. For the same issue in the same dimension, combine supporting spans in the concise reason and use one representative exact quote; do not split consecutive sentences into duplicate defects or assign both noncritical and critical severity. Do not suppress distinct critical types merely because they occur in the same sentence.

An unsupported material assertion is a content defect when the rubric says so, not an input problem. Use input_problem only when missing or contradictory required inputs genuinely prevent assessment, and explain the obstacle. Never use input_problem to imply acceptance.

task.brief:
FROZEN PERSONA
# Frozen Marketing persona profile

- Audience: the English-speaking owner-operator of a 1-10-person small business who has
  tried ChatGPT but has not integrated AI into a real workflow.
- Decision context: the owner compares a bounded automation investment with continuing
  manual work or hiring; final approval and business authority remain human.
- Voice: a plain-speaking technical expert addressing another founder directly. Trust and
  operational specificity take priority over enthusiasm.
- Evidence boundary: never imply customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, revenue lift,
  production readiness, or capabilities beyond the supplied evidence.
- Practicality: explain one observable workflow decision, threshold, diagnostic question,
  control, or next step. Do not force AI where it is unsuitable.
- Style: English, restrained, no hype, no fabricated urgency, no unsupported numbers, and
  no more than one understated humorous phrase.
- CTA: use none unless the task explicitly authorises one. If authorised, place at most one
  primary CTA at the end and never imply scarcity.
- Identity: Bareni is an employee-free consulting practice being built by the study author;
  self-built demos are not customer case studies.


APPROVED TASK
**Audience:** CEO of a 1-10-person small business.
**Owner-specified abstract topic:** AI disclosure as a design constraint
**Task:** Turn the abstract topic into a bounded Bareni workflow decision. Explain one practical next step.
**Format pattern:** CF-03.
**Persona focus:** PF-03_evidence_and_boundary.
**Evidence boundary:** Use only approved Bareni evidence. Do not invent customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, capabilities, or a multi-person team.
**CTA rule:** None.
**Output:** English LinkedIn post; body target 1200-1500 characters, hard range 150-2000; title stored separately.
required: Address the owner-specified topic as one concrete, bounded workflow decision.
Explain one practical next step for the owner.
prohibited: No invented customer, deployment, result, number, capability, multi-person team, or sales CTA.
No autonomous money movement or high-risk decision; no excluded service.
preserve: Preserve the frozen persona, approved evidence status, and human approval boundaries.
Use plain English; keep examples or proposals distinct from existing capabilities or observed results.

company_evidence.text:
## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

steps.instruction: Define AI disclosure as a control requirement, not a product feature. Frame it for the owner as: which workflow decisions must be flagged to the customer as AI-assisted, and who (you or the customer) makes the final approval.

Test disclosure clarity in a pilot with one customer segment or workflow task. Ask: does the customer understand where AI helps and where you decide?
Separate the disclosure UI (badge, label, or prompt) from the automation logic. Keep them independent so policy changes do not require code rewrites.
Document the disclosure rule once and reuse it across workflows. Make it a checklist item in your pilot proposal and handoff, so every customer knows the boundary from the start.

draft.title: Requirement freeze is a control, not a trap
draft.body:
If you run a small business, requirement freeze is worth revisiting in one narrow place: the workflow that changed after you wrote it down. That is usually where friction shows up first. A repeat task starts needing exceptions, but the SOP or automation still assumes the old rule. Then the real choice is simple: keep the frozen spec and handle exceptions manually, update the spec and rebuild the workflow, or design the process so exceptions are flagged for human review. That third option is a design choice to be scoped, not a claim that software can decide for itself.

Bareni’s diagnostic approach fits this kind of decision. Identify one recurring workflow. Be honest about whether AI fits. If it does, define scope and measures before anything is built. No mystery there; the mystery is usually the spreadsheet.

The practical threshold is not a magic number. It is the point where exceptions are no longer rare enough to ignore. If you are spending more and more time on exceptions, the frozen requirement is no longer protecting the process; it is hiding the gap between the process on paper and the process in real life.

One useful next step: pick one documented workflow and ask, “What has changed since we froze this, and how many exceptions did I make this week?” If the answer is “too many to count,” the spec is probably frozen in the wrong place. Human approval still owns any scope change, especially where money or other high-risk decisions are involved.

# Frozen Marketing persona profile

- Audience: the English-speaking owner-operator of a 1-10-person small business who has
  tried ChatGPT but has not integrated AI into a real workflow.
- Decision context: the owner compares a bounded automation investment with continuing
  manual work or hiring; final approval and business authority remain human.
- Voice: a plain-speaking technical expert addressing another founder directly. Trust and
  operational specificity take priority over enthusiasm.
- Evidence boundary: never imply customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, revenue lift,
  production readiness, or capabilities beyond the supplied evidence.
- Practicality: explain one observable workflow decision, threshold, diagnostic question,
  control, or next step. Do not force AI where it is unsuitable.
- Style: English, restrained, no hype, no fabricated urgency, no unsupported numbers, and
  no more than one understated humorous phrase.
- CTA: use none unless the task explicitly authorises one. If authorised, place at most one
  primary CTA at the end and never imply scarcity.
- Identity: Bareni is an employee-free consulting practice being built by the study author;
  self-built demos are not customer case studies.

selected_lessons.application: The task explicitly specifies 'CTA rule: None,' so no booking prompt or meeting invitation is permitted. The post must end with a practical observation or diagnostic question that invites the reader to think, not to act. L01 reinforces this by treating any implicit CTA as prohibited in informational content.

steps.instruction: Translate the abstract topic 'rethinking requirement freeze' into a single, concrete workflow decision relevant to a 1-10-person business owner. Identify one observable moment in the owner's routine where a frozen specification (unchanged requirements, locked scope) creates friction or delay—for example, a customer request that falls outside documented process, or a repetitive task whose rules changed but the automation logic did not.

Define the bounded decision: does the owner keep the frozen spec and manage exceptions manually, update the spec and rebuild the automation, or design the system to detect and flag exceptions for human review without rebuilding? Anchor the choice to Bareni's diagnostic practice: identify the one recurring workflow, confirm whether AI fits, and define scope and measures honestly.

Explain the practical threshold that triggers the decision: for example, 'if manual exception handling is growing beyond X hours per week, the cost of updating the automation becomes justified.' Use only approved Bareni language—no invented results or benchmarks—and reference human approval authority over scope changes.

State the practical next step: a diagnostic question the owner can ask themselves or bring to a discussion. Example: 'Which of your documented workflows has changed most since you set it up? How many times this week did you make an exception?' Avoid proposing a meeting or booking; use a neutral, self-directed framing.

Close with a plain-language observation about why frozen requirements matter for automation: they reduce surprises and cost, but they also hide the gap between intention and reality. Offer no CTA, urgency, or scarcity; instead, position the reflection as a normal part of small-business operations.

Verify that the draft contains no invented customers, customer results, guaranteed savings, multi-person team, or legal registration of Bareni; that human approval is preserved for scope changes; and that Bareni is described only as a consulting practice being built by the thesis author. Confirm the character count falls within the hard range of 150–2000 and targets 1200–1500.

constraints_to_preserve.handling: Select no invented customers, deployments, results, numbers, or multi-person teams. Treat the decision and next step as generic guidance, not a customer case study or capability claim.
Preserve human approval for scope changes and cost decisions. Do not propose autonomous system updates or high-risk actions; frame all decisions as owner-controlled.
Maintain the frozen persona (owner-operator, bounded investment mindset, human authority). Use only approved evidence status. Apply L01 to enforce the absence of a CTA.

Use plain English and explain jargon immediately. Keep the proposal distinct from existing Bareni capabilities (the three self-built demos) by framing it as guidance, not a proven product. Preserve tone: direct, technical, trustworthy, at most one restrained dry-humour phrase, no hype.

Generic but usable advice, minor stylistic weaknesses, lack of a sales CTA, and lack of inline citations are not automatically defects. A merely improvable but acceptable post must have an empty defect list.

An omission must identify a requirement that actually applies and remains missing from the whole post. If the issue satisfies an explicit critical rule, select that R-C rule; do not downgrade it because a different sentence suggests a harmless test or retains human review. Distinguish a local setting error in an explicitly hypothetical specification from a claim that the company or its prototype actually possesses an unimplemented capability. An unsupported material assertion is a content defect when the rubric says so, not an input problem. Use input_problem only when missing or contradictory required inputs genuinely prevent assessment, and explain the obstacle. Never use input_problem to imply acceptance.

draft.title: What subscription sprawl is really hiding
draft.body:
Subscription sprawl usually looks like a cost problem, but in a small business it often hides a workflow problem. The real question is not “which tool can we cancel?” It is “which subscription is only there because a person is still doing the work by hand?”

A useful first pass is simple: list every tool, what it is used for, how often it is actually touched, and which recurring task would stop if that tool disappeared. Then separate active dependencies from legacy extras. The surprising part is how often the monthly fee is not the main cost; the hidden cost is the owner time wrapped around it.

For a founder, the decision boundary is one repeatable workflow. Example only: emails arrive, data gets copied into a CRM, and a second tool is used to chase the next step. If that pattern repeats weekly and the outcome is clear, it may be worth testing whether a bounded automation can handle the routine part. If it is irregular, messy, or tied to sensitive financial, legal, medical, or bulk cold-email work, leave it alone.

Bareni is a one-person consulting practice being built to work inside the customer’s environment. Finished code and accounts are handed over as policy, with human approval kept in place for money movement and other high-risk decisions. No magic, just fewer tabs open in the browser.

The practical next step is to write down one recurring workflow and ask: are we paying for software, or for manual work that software failed to remove?

task.brief:
FROZEN PERSONA
# Frozen Marketing persona profile

- Audience: the English-speaking owner-operator of a 1-10-person small business who has
  tried ChatGPT but has not integrated AI into a real workflow.
- Decision context: the owner compares a bounded automation investment with continuing
  manual work or hiring; final approval and business authority remain human.
- Voice: a plain-speaking technical expert addressing another founder directly. Trust and
  operational specificity take priority over enthusiasm.
- Evidence boundary: never imply customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, revenue lift,
  production readiness, or capabilities beyond the supplied evidence.
- Practicality: explain one observable workflow decision, threshold, diagnostic question,
  control, or next step. Do not force AI where it is unsuitable.
- Style: English, restrained, no hype, no fabricated urgency, no unsupported numbers, and
  no more than one understated humorous phrase.
- CTA: use none unless the task explicitly authorises one. If authorised, place at most one
  primary CTA at the end and never imply scarcity.
- Identity: Bareni is an employee-free consulting practice being built by the study author;
  self-built demos are not customer case studies.


APPROVED TASK
**Audience:** CEO of a 1-10-person small business.
**Owner-specified abstract topic:** what subscription sprawl hides
**Task:** Turn the abstract topic into a bounded Bareni workflow decision. Explain one practical next step.
**Format pattern:** CF-03.
**Persona focus:** PF-01_problem_awareness.
**Evidence boundary:** Use only approved Bareni evidence. Do not invent customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, capabilities, or a multi-person team.
**CTA rule:** None.

company_evidence.text:
## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

steps.instruction: Identify subscription sprawl as a hidden cost driver: map the owner's current SaaS stack (tools, frequency of use, actual cost per month) and separate active workflow dependencies from legacy or marginal subscriptions. This surfaces the decision boundary: which subscriptions fund recurring manual work that could be automated instead of replaced?

Define the one repeatable, measurable workflow hidden in subscription sprawl—for example, manual data entry from customer emails into a CRM, or repeated approval steps across multiple tools. State the current cost (subscription + owner time) and the decision threshold: is this worth a bounded automation investment or continued manual work?

Explain the diagnostic question: does this workflow repeat at least weekly, involve no excluded services (medical, legal, high-sensitivity financial, bulk cold email), and produce a measurable outcome the owner controls? If yes, AI-plus-workflow automation may be worth a free 30-minute diagnostic to test fit and scope a fixed-price pilot.

State the next step honestly: the owner either (a) continues paying for subscriptions and manual work, (b) hires to reduce manual work, or (c) books a free diagnostic to understand whether a small automation investment could eliminate the manual task without adding new subscription costs or complexity.

Maintain trust and operational clarity by disclosing the Bareni model: one-person consulting practice, working inside the owner's environment, no fabricated urgency or guarantees, customer retains all accounts and code, and human approval is mandatory for any money movement or high-risk decision.

Close with a single soft closing sentence (no hard CTA, no scarcity language) that acknowledges the decision remains the owner's and reinforces the bounded, practical scope: the question is not whether to automate everything, but whether one specific, repeatable workflow is worth diagnosing.

output.title: What subscription sprawl is really hiding
output.body:
Subscription sprawl usually looks like a cost problem, but in a small business it often hides a workflow problem. The real question is not which tool to cancel. It is which subscription exists because someone is still doing part of the work by hand.

A useful first pass is simple: list every tool, what it is used for, how often it is actually touched, and what recurring task would stop if it disappeared. Then separate active dependencies from legacy extras. Often the monthly fee is not the main cost; the hidden cost is owner time wrapped around manual steps.

The decision boundary is one repeatable workflow. Example only: emails arrive, data is copied into a CRM, and a second tool is used to chase the next step. If that pattern repeats at least weekly, produces a measurable outcome, and stays outside excluded work like medical, legal, high-sensitivity financial, bulk cold email, scan-heavy OCR-dependent, or unsupported compliance work, it may be worth asking whether a bounded automation fits. The question is not whether to automate everything. It is whether one specific workflow is worth diagnosing.

Bareni is a one-person consulting practice being built inside the customer’s environment. Finished code and customer-named accounts are handed over as policy and no-lock-in positioning, while human approval stays in place for money movement and other high-risk decisions. That part should stay boring.

For a founder, the next step is to write down one recurring workflow and decide whether you want to keep paying for software, keep paying for manual work, or test a small automation instead.

draft.title: When definitions drift, start with one workflow
draft.body:
If your team keeps using the same word three different ways, that is usually not a “system problem” yet. It is a workflow problem. The practical question is simple: which one repeating process shows signs that the same field, label, or category is being interpreted differently each time? That could be invoices, customer records, handoffs, or even email triage. Pick one. Do not try to clean up the whole business in one sweep; that is how small problems become expensive hobbies.

The next step is to count the drift, not guess it. For two weeks, track every time the team has to recategorise something, ask for clarification, fix a duplicate record, or rework an approval because the definition was unclear. Use actual instances, not a feeling that it is “a lot.” Once you can see where the rework sits, you can decide whether the fix is a clearer rule, a better template, or a grounded assistant that checks approved definitions in company documents before anything moves forward.

That fit check matters. If the task needs human judgment, policy sign-off, or context outside the written rule, AI is a helper, not a replacement. And for anything involving money movement or other high-risk decisions, the owner still approves it. At Bareni, we keep that boundary explicit: the tool can flag drift, but it should not quietly decide what your business means.

draft.title: What subscription sprawl is really hiding
draft.body:
Subscription sprawl usually looks like a cost problem, but in a small business it often hides a workflow problem. The real question is not “which tool can we cancel?” It is “which subscription is only there because a person is still doing the work by hand?”

A useful first pass is simple: list every tool, what it is used for, how often it is actually touched, and which recurring task would stop if that tool disappeared. Then separate active dependencies from legacy extras. The surprising part is how often the monthly fee is not the main cost; the hidden cost is the owner time wrapped around it.

For a founder, the decision boundary is one repeatable workflow. Example only: emails arrive, data gets copied into a CRM, and a second tool is used to chase the next step. If that pattern repeats weekly and the outcome is clear, it may be worth testing whether a bounded automation can handle the routine part. If it is irregular, messy, or tied to sensitive financial, legal, medical, or bulk cold-email work, leave it alone.

Bareni is a one-person consulting practice being built to work inside the customer’s environment. Finished code and accounts are handed over as policy, with human approval kept in place for money movement and other high-risk decisions. No magic, just fewer tabs open in the browser.

The practical next step is to write down one recurring workflow and ask: are we paying for software, or for manual work that software failed to remove?

steps.instruction: Identify subscription sprawl as a hidden cost driver: map the owner's current SaaS stack (tools, frequency of use, actual cost per month) and separate active workflow dependencies from legacy or marginal subscriptions. This surfaces the decision boundary: which subscriptions fund recurring manual work that could be automated instead of replaced?

Define the one repeatable, measurable workflow hidden in subscription sprawl—for example, manual data entry from customer emails into a CRM, or repeated approval steps across multiple tools. State the current cost (subscription + owner time) and the decision threshold: is this worth a bounded automation investment or continued manual work?

Explain the diagnostic question: does this workflow repeat at least weekly, involve no excluded services (medical, legal, high-sensitivity financial, bulk cold email), and produce a measurable outcome the owner controls? If yes, AI-plus-workflow automation may be worth a free 30-minute diagnostic to test fit and scope a fixed-price pilot.

State the next step honestly: the owner either (a) continues paying for subscriptions and manual work, (b) hires to reduce manual work, or (c) books a free diagnostic to understand whether a small automation investment could eliminate the manual task without adding new subscription costs or complexity.

Maintain trust and operational clarity by disclosing the Bareni model: one-person consulting practice, working inside the owner's environment, no fabricated urgency or guarantees, customer retains all accounts and code, and human approval is mandatory for any money movement or high-risk decision.

Close with a single soft closing sentence (no hard CTA, no scarcity language) that acknowledges the decision remains the owner's and reinforces the bounded, practical scope: the question is not whether to automate everything, but whether one specific, repeatable workflow is worth diagnosing.

An omission must identify a requirement that actually applies and remains missing from the whole post. draft.title: Requirement freeze should be a control, not a prison
draft.body:
If you run a small business, requirement freeze is worth rethinking in one narrow place: the workflow that changed after you wrote it down. In practice, that is usually where the pain shows up first — a repeat task starts needing exceptions, but the automation or SOP still assumes the old rule. Then the choice is not “AI or no AI.” It is more ordinary than that: keep the frozen spec and handle exceptions manually, update the spec and rebuild the workflow, or design the process to flag exceptions for human review. That third option is a design choice, not a claim that the system can decide for itself.

Bareni’s diagnostic approach fits this kind of decision: identify one recurring workflow, be honest about whether AI fits, and define scope and measures before anything is built. For a founder, the useful threshold is not a magic number. It is the point where exceptions are no longer rare enough to ignore. If you are spending more and more time on exceptions, the frozen requirement is no longer protecting you; it is hiding the gap between the process on paper and the process in real life.

A practical next step is simple: pick one documented workflow and ask, “What has changed since we froze this, and how many exceptions did I make this week?” If the answer is “too many to count,” the spec may be frozen in the wrong place. Human approval still owns any scope change, especially where money or other high-risk decisions are involved.

task.brief:
FROZEN PERSONA
# Frozen Marketing persona profile

- Audience: the English-speaking owner-operator of a 1-10-person small business who has
  tried ChatGPT but has not integrated AI into a real workflow.
- Decision context: the owner compares a bounded automation investment with continuing
  manual work or hiring; final approval and business authority remain human.
- Voice: a plain-speaking technical expert addressing another founder directly. Trust and
  operational specificity take priority over enthusiasm.
- Evidence boundary: never imply customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, revenue lift,
  production readiness, or capabilities beyond the supplied evidence.
- Practicality: explain one observable workflow decision, threshold, diagnostic question,
  control, or next step. Do not force AI where it is unsuitable.
- Style: English, restrained, no hype, no fabricated urgency, no unsupported numbers, and
  no more than one understated humorous phrase.
- CTA: use none unless the task explicitly authorises one. If authorised, place at most one
  primary CTA at the end and never imply scarcity.
- Identity: Bareni is an employee-free consulting practice being built by the study author;
  self-built demos are not customer case studies.


APPROVED TASK
**Audience:** CEO of a 1-10-person small business.
**Owner-specified abstract topic:** rethinking requirement freeze
**Task:** Turn the abstract topic into a bounded Bareni workflow decision. Explain one practical next step.
**Format pattern:** CF-01.
**Persona focus:** PF-03_evidence_and_boundary.
**Evidence boundary:** Use only approved Bareni evidence. Do not invent customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, capabilities, or a multi-person team.
**CTA rule:** None.
**Output:** English LinkedIn post; body target 1200-1500 characters, hard range 150-2000; title stored separately.
required: Address the owner-specified topic as one concrete, bounded workflow decision.
Explain one practical next step for the owner.
prohibited: No invented customer, deployment, result, number, capability, multi-person team, or sales CTA.
No autonomous money movement or high-risk decision; no excluded service.
preserve: Preserve the frozen persona, approved evidence status, and human approval boundaries.
Use plain English; keep examples or proposals distinct from existing capabilities or observed results.

company_evidence.text:
## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:
  a 90-day execution roadmap, success measures, build-versus-buy decision, and
  tool selection.
- Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start. Retainer support is optional.
  Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

## Demonstrated systems and boundaries

### Knowledge assistant

- Self-built local demo using synthetic Acme Shop data. It can ingest MD, PDF, and
  URL content; perform vector search and reranking; generate grounded LLM answers;
  and show sources. It works end to end locally, but the deployed public route is
  locked. Automated testing, rate limiting, and billing are planned, not working.
- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

steps.instruction: Translate the abstract topic 'rethinking requirement freeze' into a single, concrete workflow decision relevant to a 1-10-person business owner. Identify one observable moment in the owner's routine where a frozen specification (unchanged requirements, locked scope) creates friction or delay—for example, a customer request that falls outside documented process, or a repetitive task whose rules changed but the automation logic did not.

Define the bounded decision: does the owner keep the frozen spec and manage exceptions manually, update the spec and rebuild the automation, or design the system to detect and flag exceptions for human review without rebuilding? Anchor the choice to Bareni's diagnostic practice: identify the one recurring workflow, confirm whether AI fits, and define scope and measures honestly.

Explain the practical threshold that triggers the decision: for example, 'if manual exception handling is growing beyond X hours per week, the cost of updating the automation becomes justified.' Use only approved Bareni language—no invented results or benchmarks—and reference human approval authority over scope changes.

State the practical next step: a diagnostic question the owner can ask themselves or bring to a discussion. Example: 'Which of your documented workflows has changed most since you set it up? How many times this week did you make an exception?' Avoid proposing a meeting or booking; use a neutral, self-directed framing.

Close with a plain-language observation about why frozen requirements matter for automation: they reduce surprises and cost, but they also hide the gap between intention and reality. Offer no CTA, urgency, or scarcity; instead, position the reflection as a normal part of small-business operations.

Verify that the draft contains no invented customers, customer results, guaranteed savings, multi-person team, or legal registration of Bareni; that human approval is preserved for scope changes; and that Bareni is described only as a consulting practice being built by the thesis author. output.title: Requirement freeze is a control, not a trap
output.body:
If you run a small business, requirement freeze is worth revisiting in one narrow place: the workflow that changed after you wrote it down. That is usually where friction shows up first. A repeat task starts needing exceptions, but the SOP or automation still assumes the old rule. Then the real choice is simple: keep the frozen spec and handle exceptions manually, update the spec and rebuild the workflow, or design the process so exceptions are flagged for human review. That third option is a design choice to be scoped, not a claim that software can decide for itself.

Bareni’s diagnostic approach fits this kind of decision. Identify one recurring workflow. Be honest about whether AI fits. If it does, define scope and measures before anything is built. No mystery there; the mystery is usually the spreadsheet.

The practical threshold is not a magic number. It is the point where exceptions are no longer rare enough to ignore. If you are spending more and more time on exceptions, the frozen requirement is no longer protecting the process; it is hiding the gap between the process on paper and the process in real life.

One useful next step: pick one documented workflow and ask, “What has changed since we froze this, and how many exceptions did I make this week?” If the answer is “too many to count,” the spec is probably frozen in the wrong place. Human approval still owns any scope change, especially where money or other high-risk decisions are involved.

draft.title: When definitions drift, start with one workflow
draft.body:
If your team keeps using the same word three different ways, that is usually not a “system problem” yet. It is a workflow problem. The practical question is simple: which one repeating process shows signs that the same field, label, or category is being interpreted differently each time? That could be invoices, customer records, handoffs, or even email triage. Pick one. Do not try to clean up the whole business in one sweep; that is how small problems become expensive hobbies.

The next step is to count the drift, not guess it. For two weeks, track every time the team has to recategorise something, ask for clarification, fix a duplicate record, or rework an approval because the definition was unclear. Use actual instances, not a feeling that it is “a lot.” Once you can see where the rework sits, you can decide whether the fix is a clearer rule, a better template, or a grounded assistant that checks approved definitions in company documents before anything moves forward.

That fit check matters. If the task needs human judgment, policy sign-off, or context outside the written rule, AI is a helper, not a replacement. And for anything involving money movement or other high-risk decisions, the owner still approves it. At Bareni, we keep that boundary explicit: the tool can flag drift, but it should not quietly decide what your business means.

## Identity and audience

- The formal name is Bareni. Never write Baren-i.
- Bareni is a consulting practice being built by the author of the thesis. It is
  not yet a legally registered company. Marketing copy does not need to announce
  the absence of customers, but it must never imply invented customers, projects,
  testimonials, deployments, or results.
- Bareni is based in Frankfurt am Main and serves English-speaking customers
  globally. English is the only current consulting, delivery, and customer-data
  language. Germany is a location, not the current target market; do not present
  German customers or German-language delivery as current services.
- The intended reader is an owner-operator of a 1–10 person small business. A
  representative scenario is a six-person D2C online shop whose owner compares an
  automation investment with the cost of another hire. The representative pains
  are 8–10 hours a week of repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads,
  and manual invoice/data work. The 8–10 hours is a persona scenario, not a market
  statistic or observed customer result.
- The best-fit reader has tried ChatGPT but has not connected AI to a business
  workflow. Especially suitable businesses already work in English, use digital
  documents and SaaS tools, and have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a
  measurable outcome.

## Offer and delivery model

- Bareni is a one-person AI development and consulting practice that automates
  repetitive work for small businesses. Public voice uses "we".
- Services include a grounded knowledge assistant; controlled accounts-payable
  automation; Atlas Partner; general document, email, CRM, and back-office
  workflows using AI plus Zapier, Make, n8n, and small amounts of custom code;
  AI adoption consulting; and hands-on design, development, and deployment.
- Customer-facing language for the hands-on service should be simple: Bareni works
  inside the customer's environment and delivers a working system. "Forward
  Deployed Engineer" may be used in specialist discussion but is not the main
  customer-facing label.
- Normal sequence: free 30-minute diagnostic; free one-page pilot proposal;
  paid working MVP in days; fixed-price pilot in weeks; then expansion and an
  optional retainer. Do not insert a mandatory roadmap gate or separate "formal
  build" stage. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.
- The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits, and—if it does—defines pilot scope, fixed price, and measures.
- Customers who want strategy only can buy the separate AI Strategy & Roadmap:

- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement

draft.title: Requirement freeze should be a control, not a prison
draft.body:
If you run a small business, requirement freeze is worth rethinking in one narrow place: the workflow that changed after you wrote it down. In practice, that is usually where the pain shows up first — a repeat task starts needing exceptions, but the automation or SOP still assumes the old rule. Then the choice is not “AI or no AI.” It is more ordinary than that: keep the frozen spec and handle exceptions manually, update the spec and rebuild the workflow, or design the process to flag exceptions for human review. That third option is a design choice, not a claim that the system can decide for itself.

Bareni’s diagnostic approach fits this kind of decision: identify one recurring workflow, be honest about whether AI fits, and define scope and measures before anything is built. For a founder, the useful threshold is not a magic number. It is the point where exceptions are no longer rare enough to ignore. If you are spending more and more time on exceptions, the frozen requirement is no longer protecting you; it is hiding the gap between the process on paper and the process in real life.

A practical next step is simple: pick one documented workflow and ask, “What has changed since we froze this, and how many exceptions did I make this week?” If the answer is “too many to count,” the spec may be frozen in the wrong place.
